       INTERVENOR BKV LAND HOLDINGS I, LLC INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE:
       BKV Land Holdings I, LLC (“BKV”) ﬁles the following initial post-hearing brief and in
support would show the following.

                                I.   INTRODUCTION

       This case has ultimately narrowed to a straightforward question: which of the
remaining viable routes best satisﬁes the Commission’s statutory obligations while avoiding
unnecessary harm to existing and actively developing land uses. The record now makes clear
that only a limited subset of routes meaningfully satisﬁes those standards.
       Among those routes, Route 894—and secondarily Route 487—emerge as the only
alternatives that consistently perform well across the Commission’s core criteria, including
cost, impacts to habitable structures, paralleling of compatible rights-of-way, and
environmental integrity. By contrast, routes that utilize Link A42 not only perform worse
under those same criteria, but uniquely and materially impair a known, ongoing large-load
development project.

                                             1
            Accordingly, the Commission should select a route that both meets the project’s
transmission needs and avoids unnecessary and avoidable conﬂicts with existing and

reasonably foreseeable land uses—speciﬁcally, Route 894 or, alternatively, Route 487.
           Routes utilizing Link A42 are not suitable for the Commission’s selection. The record
demonstrates that these routes do not outperform the leading alternatives on any of the
Commission’s primary criteria, including cost, impacts to landowners, or compatibility with
existing land uses. More importantly, they uniquely impose severe and irreconcilable
impacts on BKV’s integrated data center and generation project.
           Where multiple viable alternatives exist that both satisfy the project’s transmission
needs and avoid these impacts, selection of a Link A42 route would be inconsistent with the
Commission’s obligation to reasonably moderate impacts on the aZected community and
to weigh competing land uses. Where the record demonstrates that certain routes create
avoidable, disproportionate impacts that are not oZset by countervailing beneﬁts, the
Commission has consistently declined to select those routes.

                                 II.    PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES1

A. Weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B),
   which proposed transmission-line route is the best alternative? (Preliminary Order
   Issue No. 8)

       1. The application and the evaluations based on it recommend the selection of
          Route 894, Route 487, or another route of interest.

           The evidence in the record conﬁrms that, when evaluated under the Commission’s
established routing factors, only a limited number of routes consistently achieve strong
performance across the relevant criteria. The application presented 122 alternative routes
for consideration. The applicants identiﬁed Route 894 as the best meets route,2 and

           Route 894
           The applicants and most of the routing experts who ﬁled testimony on behalf of the
intervenors identiﬁed Route 894 as the route that performs well on all routing criteria and on
the most important factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)
because of the following:5

               property lines, for nearly 44 percent of its overall length, which is 15.1 percent less
               than the route with greatest percentage of its length parallel to existing
               compatible rights of way and just above the median percentage.
           •   Route 894 is only 9.18 miles longer than the shortest route and just shorter than
               the median length of all the alternative routes.
           •   Route 894 best addresses environmental integrity.

           In sum, Route 894 represents a consistently high-performing route across all primary
criteria. It remains among the lowest-cost alternatives, minimizes impacts to habitable
structures relative to most routes, and achieves a balanced level of parallelism with existing
compatible rights-of-way. Critically, no record evidence demonstrates that Route 894

        Considering Costs
        Under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), cost is an important—but not determinative—
consideration. The Commission’s precedent makes clear that lower cost alone does not
justify selection where a marginal increase in cost results in materially reduced impacts to
landowners, environmental resources, or existing land uses. Accordingly, the relevant
inquiry is not which route is cheapest, but whether any incremental cost is justiﬁed by
corresponding beneﬁts under the statutory criteria. It would be inappropriate to select a
route that costs somewhat less if alternative routes that cost more have fewer impacts and
are constructable.10

and Route 469, which is least expensive of the 122 proposed alternative routes.11

            Considering Habitable Structures
           The number of habitable structures aZected by a route is one of the most direct

measures of its impact on the aZected community and is routinely aZorded signiﬁcant
weight by the Commission. It typically correlates with community values and should be
taken into account when considering the transmission line’s impact on the aZected

notice,13 and the application requires an applicant to list and map all the habitable structures
within the vicinity of a proposed segment.14 The following table provides the total number of
habitable structures for Route 894, Route 487, Route 410, which is the best performing of

parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way, including existing transmission lines,

public roads and highways, railroads, and apparent property lines. This is an important
consideration because “[p]aralleling existing ROW minimizes the intrusion of the 200-foot

           Considering Length
           The Commission has given great weight to the length of a route in prior proceedings.18

future maintenance costs, . . . determines the amount of land that will be disturbed by
construction and burdened by easements,” and illustrates the potential environmental,
cultural, or aesthetic impacts.20 The following table provides the length of Route 894,

            Summary
           In every routing case, the statutory and regulatory considerations provided in PURA

§ hm.klg(c) and jg TAC § el.jkj(b)(h)(B) must be considered. However, the Commission is not
required to give equal weight to each criteria in every instance, and it is to use its expertise
in considering and weighing the routing criteria in order to best accommodate the varying
interests involved regarding a particular proposed transmission line project.23 In weighing all
of the factors with particular consideration of the highest-weighted criteria discussed above,
it is clear Route nfi should be selected because it is amongst the shortest and least
expensive of the alternative routes, has among the lowest number of habitable structures
within lkk feet of its centerline, and parallels existing compatible rights-of-way and property
boundaries for nearly ii percent of its length.24 However, if the Administrative Law Judges
choose to weigh the factors diZerently, then Route inm also provides a reasonable balance
of the statutory and regulatory considerations because it is also amongst the shortest and
least expensive of the alternative routes and parallels existing compatible rights-of-way and
property boundaries for nearly lk percent of its length.25

       2. Consideration of the potential impacts to BKV requires the Commission to
          avoid selecting a route that abects BKV.

           The application and related evaluations demonstrate, as briefed above, the suitability
of routes such as Routes 894 and 487 for the transmission line’s route. As the record
evidence has developed and the aZected community and routing experts have provided

the same time, the inappropriateness of selecting a route that utilizes Link A42 has become
more pronounced.
           The application and routing evaluations do not account for the presence or impacts
of BKV’s project.26 While that omission is understandable given the timing of the
transmission line project, it renders the initial comparative analysis incomplete for purposes
of ﬁnal route selection.
           Once the Commission incorporates record evidence regarding the BKV property and
project, the relative performance of routes utilizing Link A42 materially worsens. Those
routes introduce unique and substantial land use conﬂicts that are not present for
Routes 894 or 487 and therefore cannot be justiﬁed under the Commission’s obligation to
consider and moderate impacts to aZected land uses. Importantly, the record also
demonstrates that technically feasible routing alternatives exist that would avoid impacts to
the BKV property and project, conﬁrming that selection of a route utilizing Link A42 is not
necessary to meet the project’s objectives and cannot be justiﬁed under the Commission’s
statutory obligations.27
           Impacts to BKV

the size of the proposed transmission line, the number of intervenors and aZected interests,

           BKV is developing a data center along Link Aie and has assembled over ikk acres
that is serving as the basis for a coordinated development.30 The project includes an
integrated, generation-supported data center and industrial load project, for which BKV has
submitted an air permit application with TCEQ and received a Large Load Application
Number after submitting to Oncor’s Conﬁdence Criteria program in Qi ekel and submitting
the Oncor Large Load Questionnaire along with an Attestation of Site Control.31 This
development is not speculative or preliminary.

including ﬁling an air permit application with the Texas Commission on Environmental
Quality, securing a Large Load Application number through Oncor’s Conﬁdence Criteria
process, placing deposits for modular generation equipment, conducting geotechnical and
environmental diligence, and advancing site layout and engineering design.33 These actions

           Critically, the assembled site is designed as an integrated development footprint and
cannot be replicated or preserved on a parcel-by-parcel basis; impairment to any portion of
the assemblage has cascading eZects on the feasibility and functionality of the entire
project.35
           The transmission line would have a severe impact on the BKV property and project if
Link Aie were utilized in the route for the transmission line. If used, Link Aie would traverse,
bisect, and impose substantial permanent easement and construction impacts on the BKV
property.36 These impacts directly implicate the Commission’s obligation to consider
compatibility with existing and reasonably foreseeable land uses and to avoid unnecessary
interference when viable alternatives exist. The transmission line impact would include but
not be limited to: (j) severing the assembled site, (e) destroying the coordinated functionality
of the project; (h) disrupting planned infrastructure corridors required for power, access, and
utilities; (i) constraining or eliminating feasible site layouts, including setbacks, safety
buZers, and operational separation; and (l) materially impairing both the usability and value
of the entire assemblage.37 These impacts are not minor, temporary, or readily mitigable and
would fundamentally undermine the feasibility of the planned development, eZectively
rendering the project infeasible.38

            The alignment for Link Aie is such that if Link Aie were utilized for the transmission
line’s route, then the property could no longer be used for BKV’s data center.39 While BKV

explored feasible alternative alignments of Link Aie that would moderate the impact of the
transmission line of BKV’s project, no alternative alignments were identiﬁed. The
transmission line and the data center are not compatible with one another.40 It is not possible
to route along Link Aie and accommodate both projects because the BKV property cannot
be used for both projects.
           Although the Commission does not assign equal weight to existing conditions and
future development, its precedent requires that ongoing and reasonably foreseeable
development be meaningfully considered and its impacts moderated where feasible. Here,
that consideration reinforces—rather than alters—the conclusion already supported by the
traditional routing factors: that routes avoiding Link Aie better satisfy the Commission’s
statutory obligations.41
           Moderating the Transmission Line’s Impacts on the Abected Community
           Routing along Link Aie would create a direct and irreconcilable conﬂict with a
signiﬁcant large-load development project, contrary to the Commission’s obligation to
moderate impacts on aZected land uses where reasonable alternatives exist. Because other
routes can satisfy the transmission need while avoiding this conﬂict, selection of a Link Aie
route would impose unnecessary and avoidable harm.42 This would be contrary to state
policy to encourage the development of large loads such as BKV’s project and cannot be

landowners. The Commission fails to do so when it selects a route that is routed over

there are alternative routes crossing properties that can accommodate both the
transmission line and the properties’ other land uses. As a result, the Commission should
not select a route which includes Link Aie.
           Routing Comparisons
           The record conﬁrms that no route utilizing Link Aie outperforms Route inm—or

inquiry is not which route is cheapest, but whether any incremental cost is justified by
corresponding benefits under the statutory criteria. It would be inappropriate to select a

route that costs somewhat less if alternative routes that cost more have fewer impacts and
are constructable.10

statutory obligations.41

policy to encourage the development of large loads such as BKV's project and cannot be
